spans.content: Melting, Processing, and Properties of Disordered Fe-Al
and Fe-Al-C Based Alloys
V.V. SATYA PRASAD,<sup>1</sup> SHIVKUMAR KHAPLE,<sup>1</sup> and R.G. BALIGIDAD<sup>1,2</sup>
1.—Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory, Kanchanbagh, Hyderabad 500058, India. 2.—e-mail
rbaligidad@yahoo.com
This article presents a part of the research work conducted in our laboratory
to develop lightweight steels based on Fe-Al alloys containing 7 wt.% and
9 wt.% aluminum for construction of advanced lightweight ground transpor-
tation systems, such as automotive vehicles and heavy-haul truck, and for civil
engineering construction, such as bridges, tunnels, and buildings. The melting
and casting of sound, porosity-free ingots of Fe-Al-based alloys was accom-
plished by a newly developed cost-effective technique. The technique consists
of using a special flux cover and proprietary charging schedule during air
induction melting. These alloys were also produced using a vacuum induction
melting (VIM) process for comparison purposes. The effect of aluminum
(7 wt.% and 9 wt.%) on melting, processing, and properties of disordered solid
solution Fe-Al alloys has been studied in detail. Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy could be
produced using air induction melting with a flux cover with the properties
comparable to the alloy produced through the VIM route. This material could
be further processed through hot and cold working to produce sheets and thin
foils. The cold-rolled and annealed sheet exhibited excellent room-tempera-
ture ductility. The role of carbon in Fe-7 wt.% Al alloys has also been exam-
ined. The results indicate that Fe-Al and Fe-Al-C alloys containing about
7 wt.% Al are potential lightweight steels.
INTRODUCTION
The iron-aluminum alloys containing 6–9 wt.%
aluminum show a reduction in density of 10% and
are popularly known as lightweight steels. These
newly developed lightweight steels show promising
physical, mechanical, and technological properties,
such as high specific elastic stiffness and strength,
excellent ductility and formability, and reduced
specific weight. In view of the aforementioned
attractive combination of properties, the light-
weight steels show promise for the construction of
advanced lightweight ground transportation sys-
tems, such as automotive vehicles and heavy-haul
trucks.
The Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory
(DMRL) has carried out extensive studies on the
development of ordered Fe-Al-C alloys containing
11 wt.% and 16 wt.% Al for the past two decades.
DMRL’s main contribution has been in the devel-
opment of the most economical melting route for
bulk production of Fe-Al-C alloys by a combination
of air induction melting (AIM) and electroslag
refining (ESR).<sup>7–9</sup> The AIM ingots exhibited exten-
sive gas porosity that could be totally eliminated by
the ESR process. Subsequently, a proprietary flux
cover and a novel charging schedule were developed
to produce sound ingots using the AIM process. We
have exhaustively evaluated the role of Al and C

It has been reported that reduction in Al content

(i) a reduced susceptibility to environmental

disordered solid solution alloy, while Fe-9 wt.% Al

MELTING OF IRON-ALUMINUM ALLOYS
Air Induction Melting of Fe-Al Alloys
AIM is the most economical melting route, and it is
widely used for bulk production of steels containing
nonreactive elements. Melting of iron-aluminum
alloys containing a large amount aluminum requires
consideration of the following factors during AIM: (i)
large difference in melting points and density
between Fe and Al, (ii) exothermic nature of the
formation of
\mathrm { { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } _ { 3 } , } }
and (iii) oxidation of Al due to its
high reactivity. Traditionally, Fe-Al alloys with
higher aluminum levels are prone to develop exten-
sive gas porosity when melted through air induction
melting
.<sup>17,18</sup> The same phenomenon was observed in
the present case of air induction melting of Fe-Al
alloys containing 7 wt.% and 9 wt.% Al.
The formation of gas porosity in the ingots may be
explained by the reaction of highly reactive alumi-
num with water vapor in the air:
\mathrm{H} _ {2} \mathrm{O} (\mathrm{V}) + 2 / 3 \mathrm{Al} = 1 / 3 \mathrm{Al} _ {2} \mathrm{O} _ {3} + 2 \mathrm{H} (\text { in   Al })\tag{1}
Moisture on the charge, refractories, and tools in
the atmosphere may be a possible source of water
vapor for the above reaction. The hydrogen gas lib-
erated by this reaction dissolves into the liquid
metal. As it cannot escape during solidification, it
results in the formation of gas porosity. For a given
concentration of hydrogen, the gas porosity in the
unit volume of iron-aluminide ingot is very high
compared with aluminum due to the relatively
higher density (6.7
\mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )
of iron-aluminum alloys.
For example, only 8 ppm of hydrogen present in
iron-aluminide ingot can result in formation of
about
\mathrm { 5 0 ~ c m ^ { 3 } }
of hydrogen gas porosity in 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of
iron-aluminide ingot at STP. Furthermore, the liq-
uidus temperature of iron-aluminum alloys is con-
siderably higher than that of aluminum. The Fe-Al
alloy ingots containing 7 wt.% Al were free from
hydrogen gas porosity, whereas alloys containing
9 wt.% aluminum showed gas porosity. The lower
gas porosity in Fe-Al alloys containing lower levels
of Al may be attributed to the presence of a low
concentration of hydrogen in the liquid metal, which
is well within the solubility limit. It may be argued
that Fe-Al alloy with lower Al content is expected to
liberate a low concentration of hydrogen compared
with the Fe-Al alloy containing a higher content of
Al. The Fe-7Al alloy ingots were also sound and free
from microcracks.

on processing of iron-aluminum alloys<sup>19,20</sup> suggests

atmosphere or vacuum, which reduces the chances
of hydrogen pick-up and, hence, gas porosity.

Air Induction Melting of Fe-Al Alloys with
Flux Cover
Although the VIM process is known to yield Fe-Al
alloy ingots free from gas porosity, the process is
expensive and not easily available. Hence, efforts
have been put into develop an alternative cost-
effective melting process to produce Fe-Al alloys
without gas porosity. The alternative process in-
volves air induction melting using a protective flux
cover and proprietary charging schedule. Sound,
porosity-free Fe-Al alloys ingots containing 7 wt.%
and 9 wt.% Al were successfully produced by this
process (Fig. 1). The 30-kg heats of Fe-Al alloys
containing 7 wt.% and 9 wt.% Al were prepared by
Inductotherm medium-frequency AIM of 50-kg
capacity. Commercial purity aluminum and iron
were used as raw material. The iron charge was
cleaned by pickling in dilute hydrochloric acid. The
iron pieces were charged into an alumina-lined
crucible. After melting the iron charge, preheated
flux containing
\mathrm { { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } _ { 3 } , } }
CaO, MgO, and
\mathrm { \bar { C } a F _ { 2 } }
was
added to provide a protective cover to the melt and
was allowed to melt. The cleaned and preheated
aluminum pieces were then plunged into the molten
iron bath. The bath was held at 1900 K for a very
short time (2 min) to prevent aluminum losses. The
melt was then top poured into split cast iron molds.
The flux cover added after melting iron charge acts
as a barrier between the aluminum in the melt and
water vapor in the air and prevents the formation
and pick-up of hydrogen by the reaction between
aluminum in the melt and water vapor in the air.
The composition of the flux cover was optimized
carefully to ensure that it refines the liquid metal
with respect to impurities and that it does not at
tack the crucible lining. During AIM, the flux must
be kept molten to allow charging of aluminum and
to aid pouring into molds. The flux does not take
part in the heat generation and is kept molten
through the heat transfer from the molten metal
beneath and by the heat released due to the highly
exothermic reaction between iron and aluminum.
Therefore, the flux charge had to be limited to an
amount that is just sufficient to provide adequate
protective cover during charging and melting of
aluminum.
Selection of crucible lining material for melting iron
aluminides is very critical in the above three pro-
cesses. This is important for two reasons: (i) to have a
long crucible life and (ii) to minimize impurity pick-up
from the crucible lining. MgO is the most common
choice for commercial steels and alloys containing a
low level of aluminum. The standard free energy data
(Fig. 2) show that Al in the melt can reduce MgO at
temperatures of about 1873 K, which is very close to
the melting point of iron aluminides.<sup>21</sup> The reduction
of MgO results in the pick-up of magnesium by the
alloy and in erosion of the crucible. It has also been
reported that high Mg levels especially when segre-
gated can cause problems in hot working.<sup>19</sup> Ingots of
both Fe-7 wt.% and 9 wt.% Al alloy were completely
free from gas porosity. The Fe-7Al alloy ingots were

Processing of Fe-Al Disordered Alloys
The 80-mm-diameter AIM, VIM, and AIMFC in-
gots of Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy and VIM and AIMFC in-
gots of 9 wt.% Al alloys were preheated in a hearth
furnace at 1373 K for 1 h and hot-forged in a 1-
tonne pneumatic forge hammer with die platens at
room temperature. The 24-mm-thick sections of the
forged billets were preheated at 1373 K for 1 h and
hot rolled by 50% with 1-mm reduction in thickness
per pass. The samples were reheated after every six
rolling passes under similar conditions as in pre-
heating. The final thickness of the hot-rolled plate
was 12 mm. Ingots of Fe-7 wt.% Al alloys produced
by all three processes exhibited excellent hot work-
ability. The Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy by VIM and AIMFC
could also be cold rolled to thin sheets and foils
(Fig. 3). Due to the presence of gas porosity, AIM
ingots containing 9 wt.% Al could not be thermo-
mechanically processed. The hot-working response
of Fe-9 wt.% Al alloy produced by AIMFC was poor.
This is in contrast to the excellent hot workability of
the same alloy produced by VIM. Microcracks were
observed in hot-rolled plates. These cracks may be
due to the presence of a high level of residual
hydrogen in the as-cast ingots (Table I), and they
may persist even after hot working. All alloys pro-
duced by the AIM, AIMFC, and VIM process
exhibited an annealed microstructure with coarse
grain size (Fig. 4). The grain size of all alloys pro-
duced by AIMFC is comparable with the grain size
of alloys produced by the VIM process (Table II).
The Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy produced by the AIM process
exhibited poor room-temperature tensile ductility
compared with AIMFC and VIM alloys. The room-
temperature tensile ductility of Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy
produced by AIMFC is comparable to the alloy
produced by VIM. The poor room-temperature duc-
tility of Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy produced by AIM may be
attributed to hydrogen embrittlement due to the
presence of a higher concentration of hydrogen
present in the AIM ingots. The presence of a higher
concentration of impurities such as oxygen and
sulfur, hence nonmetallic inclusions based on these
elements (oxides and sulfur), may also be considered
responsible for the poor room-temperature ductility
of the Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy produced by AIM. The Fe-
9 wt.% Al alloy produced by AIMFC failed at very
low stress levels during the tensile test without
exhibiting any significant elongation, whereas the
same alloy produced by VIM exhibited about 9%
total elongation. The poor room-temperature duc-
tility of the alloy produced by AIMFC may be
attributed to the presence of microcracks in the al-
loy. These microcracks are a result of hydrogen
embrittlement due to the presence of a high con-
centration of hydrogen (Table I) present in the al-
loys. Table III summarizes the room-temperature
tensile property data of a cold-rolled and annealed
sheet of 2-mm thickness of Fe-7Al alloy produced by
the AIMFC process. It can be observed that the alloy
exhibited excellent ductility values of about 40%.
The present study clearly demonstrates that the
AIMFC process can be successfully used to produce
low-carbon Fe-Al alloys when the aluminum is
about 7 wt.% with properties comparable to the al-
loys produced by VIM. The AIMFC process is less
expensive and more universally available. This low-
carbon Fe-7 wt.% Al can be cold rolled to thin sheets

CONCLUSION
A cost-effective ingot metallurgy route comprising
air induction melting with a flux cover for produc-
tion of clean and sound ingots of Fe-Al alloys con-
taining 7 wt.% has been developed. Alloy produced
by AIMFC exhibited superior properties compared
with alloy produced by the AIM process. The prop-
erties of the alloy produced by AIMFC and VIM
were comparable. Fe-9 wt.% Al alloy produced by
AIM exhibited gas porosity, whereas alloy produced
by AIMFC and VIM were free from gas porosity.
However, the alloy produced by AIMFC still exhib-
ited microcracks. It has been demonstrated that the
alloy Fe-9 wt.% Al can be produced by VIM only.
Increasing carbon in Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy resulted in
significant improvement in strength but adversely
affected ductility.

Melting, Processing, and Properties of Disordered Fe-Al and Fe-Al-C Based Alloys
CONCLUSION
A cost-effective ingot metallurgy route comprising
air induction melting with a flux cover for produc-
tion of clean and sound ingots of Fe-Al alloys con-
taining 7 wt.% has been developed. Alloy produced
by AIMFC exhibited superior properties compared
with alloy produced by the AIM process. The prop-
erties of the alloy produced by AIMFC and VIM
were comparable. Fe-9 wt.% Al alloy produced by
AIM exhibited gas porosity, whereas alloy produced
by AIMFC and VIM were free from gas porosity.
However, the alloy produced by AIMFC still exhib-
ited microcracks. It has been demonstrated that the
alloy Fe-9 wt.% Al can be produced by VIM only.
Increasing carbon in Fe-7 wt.% Al alloy resulted in
significant improvement in strength but adversely
affected ductility.
